title: Memory Pressure Detection (Linux)
exclusions: Detects sustained host-level memory and swap pressure from the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux `vmstat` feed. It does not identify the process responsible for consumption, detect cgroup or container limits, diagnose NUMA imbalance, or replace application-memory telemetry. Suppress only approved hosts and time-bounded maintenance windows in `linux_capacity_exceptions.csv`.
evidence: Saved search `linux_memory_pressure_5m`, its alert history, the "Linux Memory Pressure" dashboard panels, and a monthly CSV export containing `_time`, `host`, `memory_pct`, `swap_pct`, and `swap_out_delta` for capacity review.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Index two consecutive synthetic `vmstat` events for one test host. Set `memUsedPct=96`, increase cumulative `pgSwapOut` from 1200 to 1250, and set `swapUsedPct=25`; the second five-minute bucket must return that host with `swap_out_delta=50`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Index benign `vmstat` events with `memUsedPct=70`, unchanged `pgSwapOut`, and `swapUsedPct=25`; the search must return no row because allocated but inactive swap without new page-outs is not sufficient evidence of current memory pressure.

dataSources: `index=os sourcetype=vmstat` events produced by the `vmstat.sh` scripted input in the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833). Required fields are `host`, `memTotalMB`, `memFreeMB`, `memUsedMB`, `memUsedPct`, `swapUsedPct`, and cumulative `pgSwapOut`. The index name is a local deployment choice; `vmstat` and the field names are supplied by the add-on.
app: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833). Install the add-on on Linux Universal Forwarders that execute the scripted input and on the search tier that supplies its search-time knowledge objects.
spl:
index=os sourcetype=vmstat host=*
| bin _time span=5m
| stats avg(memUsedPct) as memory_pct avg(swapUsedPct) as swap_pct max(pgSwapOut) as swap_pages_out by _time host
| sort 0 host _time
| streamstats current=f window=1 last(swap_pages_out) as previous_swap_pages_out by host
| eval swap_out_delta=case(isnull(previous_swap_pages_out),0,swap_pages_out>=previous_swap_pages_out,swap_pages_out-previous_swap_pages_out,true(),null())
| where memory_pct>=95 OR (swap_pct>=20 AND swap_out_delta>0)
description: Detects Linux hosts with either five-minute average memory use at or above 95 percent, or swap use at or above 20 percent while the cumulative page-out counter is still increasing. Results are grouped by host and five-minute bucket so responders can distinguish active reclaim pressure from harmless historical swap allocation.
value: Early warning of active memory pressure gives Linux operators time to stop a leak, reschedule a workload, or add capacity before the kernel invokes the out-of-memory killer and disrupts services. Requiring fresh page-out activity reduces pages caused by swap that remains allocated after a past spike.
implementation: Deploy Splunkbase app 833, enable its `vmstat.sh` scripted input at a 60-second interval into an approved `os` index, and verify all required fields before saving the search. Run every five minutes over at least ten minutes of data; tune the 95-percent memory and 20-percent swap thresholds by host class.
visualization: Build a timechart of `memory_pct` and `swap_pct` by host, a table sorted by `swap_out_delta`, and single-value panels for hosts currently breaching each condition. Link each host to process, OOM-kill, and deployment-change searches; do not combine percentages and page counts on one unlabelled axis.
cimSpl:
| tstats summariesonly=t latest(Performance.mem) as mem_mb latest(Performance.mem_used) as mem_used_mb latest(Performance.swap) as swap_mb latest(Performance.swap_used) as swap_used_mb from datamodel=Performance.Memory by Performance.dest span=5m
| eval memory_pct=if(mem_mb>0,round(100*mem_used_mb/mem_mb,1),null()), swap_pct=if(swap_mb>0,round(100*swap_used_mb/swap_mb,1),0)
| where memory_pct>=95 OR swap_pct>=20
| rename Performance.dest as host
dataModelAcceleration: If using the CIM alternative, install compatible CIM knowledge objects, verify that the Performance.Memory dataset populates `mem`, `mem_used`, `swap`, and `swap_used`, and accelerate the Performance data model for longer than the search window. The CIM search cannot reproduce `pgSwapOut` activity unless that counter is separately normalized, so it is a broader capacity signal rather than an exact substitute for the raw search.

references.title: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (Splunkbase 833)
Configure data collection on forwarders with inputs.conf

knownFalsePositives:
1. **Recently reduced workload** — Linux can retain swap allocations after pressure has ended. Distinguish it by requiring `swap_out_delta>0`; do not alert on `swapUsedPct` alone.

2. **Planned load test or in-memory cache warm-up** — Confirm the host and time window in the change record, then add a host-specific entry with an expiry to `linux_capacity_exceptions.csv`.

3. **Counter reset after reboot** — `pgSwapOut` drops when a host restarts. The search emits null for a decreasing counter; correlate with `index=os sourcetype=boot` before treating the discontinuity as pressure.

4. **Fleet-wide package or backup job** — A scheduled job may legitimately consume memory on many hosts at once. Compare affected hosts with the scheduler inventory and suppress the named job window rather than excluding the metric permanently.

**Suppression mechanism:** add `| lookup linux_capacity_exceptions.csv host OUTPUT start_time end_time reason` and retain only rows outside a matching time window. Reject entries without an expiry and retain changes in change control.
reviewer: documentation review against Splunk primary sources
detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites

Use the supported Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833), not an unrelated Splunkbase application. Confirm that the add-on version supports the Splunk Enterprise or Splunk Cloud search tier in use. Test an add-on upgrade outside production because the Splunkbase listing warns that version 6.0 changed defaults and configuration files.

Create or confirm the `os` event index. The name `os` is a catalogue convention, not a requirement imposed by Splunk; if your deployment uses another index, change both the input and search. Grant the deployment-server role permission to distribute the input app, and grant the search role access only to the selected operating-system index.

## 1. Configure collection

Place local overrides in `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/Splunk_TA_nix/local/inputs.conf` on the deployment app. Do not edit the add-on's `default` directory. Enable the existing `vmstat.sh` stanza supplied by the add-on, set a 60-second interval, set `sourcetype=vmstat`, and route it to the chosen index. Preserve the exact stanza path from the installed add-on rather than inventing a new collector path.

After deployment, restart or reload the Universal Forwarder as required by the documented configuration workflow. On a representative host run `splunk btool inputs list --debug` and confirm that the winning `vmstat.sh` stanza comes from the local configuration. Search `index=os sourcetype=vmstat earliest=-10m` and verify one event per collection interval.

Do not proceed until `host`, `memTotalMB`, `memFreeMB`, `memUsedMB`, `memUsedPct`, `swapUsedPct`, and `pgSwapOut` are numeric. Compare the newest values with `vmstat -s` and `free -m` on the same host. The add-on's memory percentage excludes reclaimable buffers/cache according to its collector logic, so it need not equal the top-line Linux "used" percentage. Document that semantic in the dashboard.

## 2. Save the detection

Save the catalogue SPL as `linux_memory_pressure_5m`. The search bins samples into five-minute windows and averages the two percentages. `pgSwapOut` is cumulative since boot; `streamstats` compares adjacent buckets to derive new page-outs. A counter decrease is treated as a reset and produces no swap-pressure row.

Schedule the alert every five minutes with a lookback of at least ten minutes so two buckets are available for the delta. Trigger when result count is greater than zero and throttle by `host` for 30 minutes. Include `_time`, `host`, `memory_pct`, `swap_pct`, and `swap_out_delta` in the notification. Start with `memory_pct>=95` and `swap_pct>=20`; baseline each host class before changing these values. A database server and a stateless web node should not automatically share a threshold.

The raw search is preferred because it combines allocation with active page-outs. The CIM alternative calculates percentages from the documented Performance.Memory capacity fields, but CIM 5.3 does not define a normalized page-out counter. Treat that version as a capacity alert, not an equivalent active-pressure detector.

## 3. Validate from documentation and synthetic events

Verify search logic with two event sequences. For the positive sequence, use one host and increasing `_time`; set `memUsedPct=96`, `swapUsedPct=25`, and increase `pgSwapOut` from 1200 to 1250. The later bucket must appear. For the negative sequence, set `memUsedPct=70`, leave `pgSwapOut` unchanged, and keep `swapUsedPct=25`. No row should appear.

Also test a reboot sequence where `pgSwapOut` falls. It must not create a large negative or positive delta. These are search-level documentation tests; record them as such and do not claim that a production workload was executed.

## 4. Operationalize

Create a dashboard with separate axes for percentages and page counts. Add drilldowns to `index=os ("Out of memory" OR "Killed process") host=$host$`, the process inventory for the host, and recent deployment changes. The first response is to determine whether pressure is growing, whether the kernel is actively paging, and which workload changed. Do not clear caches or kill processes automatically from this alert.

Archive monthly results for capacity review and retain alert history under the organization's normal operations-evidence policy. The evidence proves that the search ran and produced rows; it does not by itself prove regulatory compliance.

## 5. Troubleshoot safely

If no events arrive, inspect the effective input with `btool`, forwarder logs, routing, and index permissions. If fields are null, verify that the add-on's search-time knowledge objects are installed on the search tier and that the event sourcetype is exactly `vmstat`. If every host appears after restart, inspect counter ordering and ensure the search sorts by `host _time` before `streamstats`. If swap remains high with zero page-outs, treat it as historical allocation and investigate only when application latency or memory use also worsens.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for a Linux server running short of usable memory and actively pushing work onto slower disk space. That gives the team time to fix a leak or move work before the machine starts killing programs.
